say.text: A 58-year-old man has a tense, tender groin lump that will not go back. He is vomiting and his pulse is fast.
What is your first step?

choices.label: Resuscitate, then take him to emergency surgery
Attempt gentle, then firm, manual reduction
Ultrasound of the groin before deciding
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what a tense, tender, irreducible swelling with vomiting means for the bowel inside it, not for the lump.
Reducing it feels like the reflex, since most groin lumps do go back. But tense, tender and irreducible with vomiting means strangulation until proven otherwise.
Forceful taxis can push gangrenous bowel back, or reduce the sac and contents en masse with the constriction still there.
So what must you learn about the bowel before you touch the lump?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the signs again: tense, tender, irreducible, vomiting. They mean the bowel is at risk before any reduction.

say.text: Imaging feels thorough, and ultrasound is the test people reach for in any groin problem.
But a clinically evident hernia is a clinical diagnosis, and this emergency turns on the bowel's viability first.
What would a scan change in the next ten minutes?

sure_note.text: You were sure. A scan delays the step that matters: possibly dead bowel needs resuscitation and surgery.

say.text: Resuscitate, then emergency surgery. Strangulation means the bowel may be non-viable and need resection, so the bowel decides the next step.
Manual reduction waits, because it can push dead bowel back into the abdomen.
A 6-month-old boy has a reducible right groin swelling that appears on crying.
Why does his hernia need no posterior wall repair?

choices.label: Child's tissues are too fragile to hold sutures
The defect is a patent processus over a normal wall
Mesh would restrict growth of the abdominal wall
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about the defect, not the operation: what is the child's sac, and how strong is his posterior wall?
This is the adult weak-wall model: a child's tissues look delicate, so repair seems unsafe.
But a child's posterior wall is normal. The problem is an open processus vaginalis, which herniotomy closes.
If the wall is normal, what does this child need repaired?

sure_note.text: You were sure, but a child is not a small adult with a weak wall. The operation follows the defect.

say.text: Mesh feels like the careful option in a growing child, since it is a foreign body that must last a lifetime.
Growth is not the reason. The child's operation is herniotomy alone, with no mesh and no posterior repair.
What does a mesh add when the posterior wall needs no reinforcement?

sure_note.text: You were sure. The child's operation is herniotomy alone.

say.text: In a child the defect is a patent processus vaginalis over a normal posterior wall, so removing the sac cures it.
Herniotomy alone, with no posterior wall repair, is the operation of choice for a child.
A 35-year-old man has a primary, reducible right inguinal hernia. His surgeon has no laparoscopic training.
Which repair do you choose?

choices.label: Open Bassini repair, the classic tissue repair
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Match the operation to the surgeon's training and to the hernia's qualifiers: primary, unilateral and reducible.
Laparoscopic repair feels like the modern default, so the newer technique seems right for any hernia.
But its place depends on the qualifiers. It suits bilateral or recurrent hernias, and primary unilateral ones in experienced hands.
Which detail in this stem bears on the surgeon's skill?

sure_note.text: You were sure. Laparoscopy is preferred for bilateral or recurrent hernias, not for every hernia.

say.text: Bassini is the name you remember for classic open repair, and older PYQs expected it.
Current practice is Lichtenstein mesh repair for an adult. Bassini sutures the conjoint tendon under tension.
Does this stem ask for the older exam key or for current practice?

sure_note.text: You were sure. Older keys said Bassini; current practice is Lichtenstein.

say.text: Lichtenstein tension-free mesh repair is the standard open repair for an adult.
A surgeon without laparoscopic training points to the open route. Laparoscopy suits experienced hands.
Laparoscopy has specific indications, not a general preference.
Which of these patients clearly favours a laparoscopic approach?

choices.label: A fit adult with bilateral hernias
Primary unilateral hernia, surgeon untrained in laparoscopy
Elderly man unfit for general anaesthesia
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Laparoscopy is chosen for particular qualifiers, not for the hernia type alone. Which option holds such a qualifier?
Laparoscopy feels like the modern choice, so a surgeon may reach for it for any hernia.
A primary unilateral hernia does not favour it. The standard open repair is Lichtenstein, and laparoscopy suits experienced hands.
Which detail in this stem is about the surgeon rather than the hernia?

sure_note.text: You were sure. Laparoscopy is not the default; the qualifiers decide.

say.text: Laparoscopy looks gentler, so an elderly patient may seem a good candidate for it.
But laparoscopic repair needs general anaesthesia and a learning curve, so an unfit patient is the wrong candidate.
What does a laparoscopic repair ask of the patient, and does this man give it?

sure_note.text: You were sure. General anaesthesia is a cost of laparoscopy, not a reason to choose it.

say.text: Bilateral hernias favour laparoscopic repair, and so does recurrence after an open repair.
Laparoscopy needs general anaesthesia and a learning curve, so you choose it for these qualifiers, not for every hernia.
You are counselling a patient before open and then laparoscopic repair. You must name the nerve most at risk in each.
Which pairing is correct?

choices.label: Open ilioinguinal; laparoscopic lateral femoral cutaneous
Open lateral femoral cutaneous; laparoscopic ilioinguinal
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask where each approach dissects: through the groin from the front, or from inside the abdomen. Which nerve sits there?
The ilioinguinal nerve is the famous groin nerve, so it feels like the answer for every repair.
It is the nerve most injured in open repair, but laparoscopy puts the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve at risk.
Does the approach change where the dissection runs, and so the nerve?

sure_note.text: You were sure. One nerve for every repair is the trap: the approach decides the nerve.

say.text: Both nerves lie in the groin, so a swap looks like a simple slip of memory.
Ilioinguinal is the open-repair nerve and lateral femoral cutaneous is the laparoscopic one.
Which approach works from the front of the groin?

sure_note.text: You were sure. Open repair injures the ilioinguinal nerve; laparoscopy the lateral femoral cutaneous.

say.text: Open repair most often injures the ilioinguinal nerve, with numbness over the root of the penis, the anterior scrotum and the upper medial thigh.
Laparoscopic repair most often injures the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, causing meralgia paraesthetica.
Three weeks after a TEP repair, a man has burning pain and tingling over the front and side of his thigh, with no weakness.
Which nerve is injured?

choices.label: Femoral nerve, the main thigh nerve
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The loss is in the skin over the thigh, with no weakness. Which nerve supplies that skin?
Ilioinguinal is the nerve you associate with groin repairs, so it feels like the nerve for any repair.
Its injury causes numbness at the root of the penis, the scrotum and the upper medial thigh, not burning over the lateral thigh.
Where does this man's sensation change?

sure_note.text: You were sure. Ilioinguinal injury lies in the groin and scrotum; this burning is over the thigh.

say.text: The femoral nerve lies in the triangle of pain, so it seems the nerve of a thigh complaint after groin surgery.
The triangle of pain holds it, but this loss is sensory skin over the thigh, which points to the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.
Is this man's problem weakness, or burning skin?

sure_note.text: You were sure. The triangle of pain holds this nerve, but the symptoms are sensory, not motor.

say.text: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve injury causes burning pain and numbness over the anterolateral thigh, called meralgia paraesthetica.
It lies in the triangle of pain and is the nerve most at risk in laparoscopic repair.
A fit man has a visible, reducible groin swelling with an expansile cough impulse.
What is your next step?

choices.label: Ultrasound of the groin before surgery
CT of the abdomen and pelvis first

say.text: A groin scan feels responsible before any operation, and ultrasound is the test for an occult hernia.
This hernia is clinically evident, and a clinically evident hernia does not need imaging.
What would the scan add to a lump you can already see?
CT is the most advanced test on the list, so it looks like the thorough choice.
CT is reserved for complicated or obscure presentations, such as suspected obstruction or strangulation in an obese patient.
Is this man's hernia complicated?
A clinically evident hernia is diagnosed on examination, so elective repair can be planned without imaging.
Ultrasound is for an occult hernia, and MRI follows if it is inconclusive.
A surgeon excises the sac and darns the posterior wall with the patient's own tissue, with no mesh.
What is this operation called?
Hernioplasty sounds like the general word for any hernia repair, so it feels like the safe name.
But hernioplasty means reinforcing the posterior wall with a prosthetic mesh. This operation uses the patient's own tissue.
What is the wall repaired with in this stem?
Herniotomy is the operation children get, so the word feels like the one for any groin repair.
Herniotomy is excision of the sac alone. Here the posterior wall is repaired too.
Is anything done to the wall in this stem?
Herniorrhaphy is herniotomy plus repair of the posterior wall with the patient's own tissue.
Herniotomy is sac excision alone; hernioplasty adds a prosthetic mesh.
What is the standard open repair for an adult with a primary inguinal hernia in current practice?
Bassini is the name in older textbooks and PYQ keys, so it feels like the standard open repair.
It is a tissue repair under tension, and current practice uses the Lichtenstein mesh repair.
Is the stem asking for the older exam key or for current practice?
Lichtenstein tension-free mesh repair is the standard open repair for adults.
Older PYQs expected Bassini; current practice is Lichtenstein, with Shouldice as the best tissue repair.
A 9-month-old boy has a reducible right groin swelling that appears when he cries and vanishes at rest.
Which operation is the choice?

choices.label: Herniotomy alone, high ligation of the sac

say.text: Lichtenstein is the adult standard, so an adult operation feels safest for any groin hernia.
A child's defect is a patent processus vaginalis over a normal posterior wall, so no mesh is needed.
What is the defect in a child, and is the posterior wall at fault?
Herniorrhaphy looks thorough: it removes the sac and repairs the wall, so it feels safer.
The child's posterior wall is normal, so repairing it adds surgery with nothing to fix.
If the wall is normal, what does the operation need to do?
Herniotomy alone is the operation of choice in a child.
It removes the patent processus, and the posterior wall is normal, so no repair is needed.
During a TAPP repair the surgeon must avoid the triangle of doom.
Which structure lies inside it?

choices.label: Femoral nerve, the main thigh nerve
External iliac vessels, which run on to the thigh
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve of the thigh

say.text: The femoral nerve is the big nerve of the groin and thigh, so it feels like the one in any dangerous triangle.
The femoral nerve lies in the triangle of pain. The triangle of doom holds the vessels.
Which of the two triangles holds the vessels?
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is the nerve people remember for laparoscopy, so it seems to fit a dangerous groin.
It belongs to the triangle of pain, not the vascular triangle of doom.
Which triangle contains the vessels, and which contains the nerves?
The triangle of doom is bounded by the vas deferens medially and the gonadal vessels laterally, and contains the external iliac vessels.
The triangle of pain lies lateral to the gonadal vessels and holds the nerves, including the lateral femoral cutaneous and femoral nerves.
Why is forceful reduction avoided when strangulation is suspected?

choices.label: It converts the hernia into an irreducible one
It is allowed once analgesia has been given
It can push dead bowel back or cause reduction en masse

say.text: Taxis is meant to make the hernia go back, so the risk seems to be getting stuck afterwards.
The real danger is the bowel. Forceful reduction can push gangrenous bowel back, or reduce sac and contents en masse.
What is the danger if dead bowel goes back into the abdomen?
Analgesia feels like the sensible step before any manipulation, so it seems to make taxis acceptable.
Pain relief does not show whether the bowel is alive, so the risk of pushing dead bowel back stays.
Does pain relief tell you whether the bowel is viable?
Forceful taxis can push gangrenous bowel back, or reduce sac and contents en masse, with the constriction still present.
So strangulation is treated by resuscitation and emergency surgery, with resection of non-viable bowel.
A surgeon reinforces the posterior wall with a polypropylene mesh.
What is the term for this repair?
Herniorrhaphy is the classic word for a posterior wall repair, so it feels like the term for any wall repair.
Herniorrhaphy uses the patient's own tissue. Reinforcement with a prosthetic mesh is hernioplasty.
What is the wall reinforced with in this stem?
Herniotomy is the word for the sac, and mesh is often placed in the same operation, so it seems to fit.
Herniotomy is sac excision alone, without any wall reinforcement.
Does this stem mention the sac, or the wall?
Hernioplasty is reinforcement of the posterior wall with a prosthetic mesh such as polypropylene.
Herniorrhaphy adds the patient's own tissue, and herniotomy is the sac alone.
Three questions settle this topic: is the bowel alive, who is the patient, and what do the qualifiers ask for?
Child: herniotomy alone. Adult primary: Lichtenstein. Bilateral or recurrent: laparoscopic. Open nerve: ilioinguinal; laparoscopic nerve: lateral femoral cutaneous.
